name: Backbone Ridge
approach: Stuart Lake Trailhead → Colchuck Lake Trail (~4 mi, 2,280 ft gain) → around the lake and up the moraine to the route base (roughly 200 ft left of Serpentine Arête); initial bushwhacking on brushy ledges until the party cliffs out and traverses up/right toward the ridge crest.
descent: Standard descent via the east ledges/summit gully shared with Serpentine Arête; in icy late-season conditions, an alternate 2-rappel line (70m rope, 60m possible) drops to Aasgard Pass.

bivy.name: Colchuck Lake
bivy.notes: The planned base camp for the route, roughly two and a quarter hours from the trailhead. Camp as close to the south end as you can — everything you save there is time you are not walking in the dark, because the moraine above the lake still adds about a thousand feet before the first pitch. The permit difficulty is why a great many parties simply climb the route in a single push from the car instead.
bivy.water: The lake, reliable all season
bivy.permit: An overnight permit for the lake's zone in the quota'd wilderness permit area is required from mid-May through October and is one of the harder ones to draw; outside that window permits are free and unlimited
bivy.capacity: Established sites along the west shore and around the south end; busy and competitive on summer weekends

bivy.name: First large flat ledge low on the ridge
bivy.notes: An emergency bivy, not a camp. It is the first genuinely flat spot after the initial pitches and is normally used as a break and gear-sorting stance, but it is somewhere to stop if a party is benighted low on the ridge. There is no water, no shelter and no easy way off from here, so treat it as a place to survive a night rather than a planned stage.
bivy.water: None — everything must be carried
bivy.capacity: One ledge, big enough for a party of two to sit out a night

itinerary: Camp at Colchuck Lake or day-push from the trailhead; alpine start to be climbing by first light. Parties consider an ~18-hour car-to-car day civilized for the grade — move efficiently to locate the descent before dark.

name: East Ridge via Aasgard Pass Route
approach: From Colchuck Lake's west side trail, follow cairns up the climbers' trail into Aasgard Pass, gaining roughly 2,200 ft in 0.75 mile. At the pass, head right/south along a short ridge above a tarn to reach Dragontail's east saddle, then cross the Snow Creek Glacier basin (typically snow-covered through late July, a mellow, low-crevasse slope) to the saddle on the east ridge, then a class-3 scramble/ridge walk to the summit.
descent: Reverse the ascent line: down-scramble to the Aasgard Pass saddle and descend the pass to Colchuck Lake, staying on the established, cairned line.

bivy.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
bivy.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
bivy.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
bivy.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

bivy.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
bivy.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.
bivy.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.

itinerary: Single push: Trailhead (3,400 ft) → Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.3 mi) → Aasgard Pass (7,841 ft) → east-ridge saddle (~8,500 ft) → summit (8,840 ft, ~6.25 mi one-way); round trip is roughly 12.5 mi, with car-to-car times reported in the 11-15 hour range depending on pace and conditions.

name: Serpentine Arête
approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FR 7601), hike the Colchuck Lake Trail ~4 mi / 2,280 ft gain to Colchuck Lake (5,574 ft). Round the lake's west shore to its south end, boulder-hop onto the Colchuck Glacier's lateral moraine, and traverse it toward the orange-colored rock marking the route start; 4th-class ledges lead up to a snow finger and the base of the technical climbing. Roughly 3 hours car-to-base at a brisk pace.
descent: Descend the sandy summit gully to the Backbone Ridge/Serpentine junction, then down via the Snow Creek Glacier side or over to Aasgard Pass, back to Colchuck Lake and out the trail.

bivy.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
bivy.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
bivy.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. The zone boundary with the Core Enchantment zone lies up toward Aasgard Pass, and a Core permit is valid in every zone, so a party unsure which side of the line it will sleep on is safest holding Core.
bivy.capacity: Two to four people on flat granite blocks and sand patches; nothing established, and the good spots are scattered rather than clustered

itinerary: Day 1: Drive to Stuart Lake TH (or backpack in with an Enchantments overnight permit), hike to Colchuck Lake, camp on the south shore. Day 2: Alpine start (2-4am), approach to route base (~3 hrs), climb the route (7-10 hrs), descend to Colchuck Lake and hike out (~13-14 hrs car-to-car total is typical for a fit party going car-to-car in a single push).

name: Early Winter Couloir
approach: From the Hairpin turn on SR-20 (east side of the Early Winters Spire formation), ascend roughly 1,500 ft of steep approach snow — often waist-deep before it firms up — to reach the couloir's mouth.
descent: The standard descent follows the West Couloir on the west side of the peak: bolted anchors lead down with about 4 rappels and some downclimbing to a fixed piton-and-nut anchor at a chockstone, passable with a single rope. Retreating directly back down Early Winter Couloir itself (rather than via the West Couloir) has no established rappel anchors, forcing ad hoc gear anchors in poor rock — the scenario implicated in the May 2025 fatal accident on this route.
itinerary: Typical single-day itinerary: pre-dawn start from the car, ~1 hr approach to the couloir base, 5-7 hrs of technical climbing to the col and summit, then descend via the West Couloir/Chockstone bolted rappels (not back down the couloir) in 2-3 hrs, aiming to be off all technical terrain well before dark.

name: East Face
approach: Middle Peak shares the same approach as South Peak: from Downey Creek Trailhead, follow the southern Ptarmigan Traverse cross-country route (Itswoot Ridge/Cub Lake, Bachelor Creek) to reach the range's ridge. Middle Gunsight's east face is a known technical objective once on the ridge; expect a multi-day glaciated approach with route-finding and bushwhacking, not a drive-up or short-trail access.
descent: Rappel the south-facing side of the peak (2 double-rope rappels, or about 4 on a single 60 m rope) to avoid the climb-back problem of ascending the east face descent.

bivy.name: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
bivy.notes: These are the camps that put the eastern peaks in range, and they are the reason parties carry a full glacier kit past Itswoot Ridge. The col between the Dana and Dome glaciers holds a couple of rock rings around 7,470 ft, and further east the Dome-Chickamin col is a genuine high camp with figures around 8,000 ft and above quoted for it. From that eastern col the Chickamin Glacier is the highway to Sinister Peak, whose North Face and Southwest Route are both reached across it, and on to the three Gunsight Range summits beyond, which are granite spires ringed by the Chickamin and Blue glaciers and among the most remote objectives in the state. Parties on the Gunsight peaks routinely cross the Chickamin twice in a day from a camp on this ground. Season is short: the glaciers are best covered from July into August, later brings open crevasses and bare ice, and there is no water, no shelter and no quick way down from any of it.
bivy.water: None running. Every drop is melted snow, and on bare ice years even that takes hunting for. Carry what you can from Cub Lake or the Itswoot Ridge creeks and plan the fuel for melting.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek register. Camp on snow, rock or ice. Pack out human waste, which matters more here than anywhere else in the zone because the meltwater below runs straight into the glacier-fed creeks.
bivy.capacity: Rock rings and cleared platforms for one or two parties at a time. At the Dome-Chickamin col there is a flat, large, windy option on the west side and a smaller, harder, calmer one on the east. Nothing else, and no toilet.

bivy.name: Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
bivy.notes: This exists because of the brush, and the brush is the single most important thing to understand about the south end. From the Downey Creek trailhead at 1,440 ft the Downey Creek trail runs about six easy forested miles to Sixmile Camp; after that the abandoned Bachelor Creek trail deteriorates badly. The first two miles are tolerable, then it crosses to the south side and turns into slide alder and avalanche deadfall, with reports of sixty or more trees over the trail and long sections where following it is closer to bushwhacking than hiking. Parties routinely take nine to eleven hours from the car to Cub Lake and a slow group with heavy packs can lose the trail entirely. Splitting the approach with a night around the 4,500 ft meadows near the head of the creek is the honest answer for anyone who is not fast, and it is why some parties choose to enter from Cascade Pass and exit here rather than the other way round, so the brush is done downhill and with lighter packs. There is a north-side line through open forest paralleling the creek that some report as better than the trail itself. Everything about this approach is harder than the above suggests: the Suiattle River Road has been closed to vehicles at about milepost 4 after flood damage, under a Forest Service order in effect April 2, 2026 through January 1, 2028 unless rescinded sooner, which leaves roughly sixteen extra road miles each way to a trailhead at mile 20. On top of that, the Forest Service's Miner's Fire order (06-05-26-17) closes the Downey Creek Trailhead, the Downey Creek Trail and the Bachelor Creek Trail from August 15 through December 31, 2026, unless rescinded sooner. The road also spent about a decade closed before reopening in 2014, so a long closure here is the normal state of affairs rather than a surprise. Confirm the road before committing to this end.
bivy.water: Bachelor Creek runs the whole way and is never the problem. The creek crossing itself can be, in high water or early season.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at Downey Creek. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but the ground is wet forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
bivy.capacity: Rough forest sites and a meadow flat near the head of the creek, party-sized only. Nothing established, no toilet.

bivy.name: Cub Lake
bivy.notes: Roughly 12 miles and about 3,900 ft of gain from the Downey Creek trailhead, reached by a steep switchbacking descent off the Bachelor Creek meadows and a walk around the north shore. Parties report anywhere from six hours to eleven getting here, which is a fair measure of how much the brush and the pack weight vary. It is the south-end hub: from the lake the trail climbs to Itswoot Ridge for Spire Point and Dome Peak, and everything on the Chickamin side including Sinister Peak and the Gunsight summits starts from the same ground. Because it is the established camp it also takes the impact, and there is a reasonable argument for camping on the ridge above instead where the ground is less worn, at the cost of carrying water. Coming out, this is where the traverse ends and the brush begins.
bivy.water: The lake, reliable all season. This is the last certain water for anyone heading up onto the ridge and glaciers, and the first on the way out.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Downey Creek trailhead. Camp 100 feet back from the shore. Practically speaking no fires, and the site is heavily enough used that the surrounding wood is already gone.
bivy.capacity: A well established camp at the lake with room for a few parties, plus meadow sites nearby. It is the most used ground in the southern half of the zone and it shows.

bivy.name: Itswoot Ridge
bivy.notes: This is the working base for the southern peaks and the camp most parties coming in from Downey Creek actually use. Camps are quoted anywhere between roughly 5,900 and 6,400 ft depending on which bench you take, so the number here describes the lower, wetter end of the ridge rather than a single spot. From the benches it is moderate snow of about thirty degrees, or a scree-and-heather line on the left in late season, up to Spire Col at 7,760 ft, and from the col a short descending traverse onto the upper Dana Glacier puts you under the southeast and southwest faces of Spire Point. Dome Peak is the other objective, reached over the Dana Glacier and the Dome Glacier above. Reaching this ridge from the car is a full day with a heavy pack, so plan on arriving late and going nowhere else that evening.
bivy.water: Small running creeks below the lower benches, fed by snowfields on the north side of the ridge, and generally dependable through the normal climbing season. The higher benches toward the col dry out first, so drop back down for water rather than assuming it is there.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek trailhead register, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle. No campfires up here.
bivy.capacity: A string of flat heather benches along the ridge rather than one site, so several parties can spread out without crowding each other. No toilet, no built platforms.

itinerary: Day 1: Downey Creek Trailhead to Bachelor Flats camp (6 miles, 3,100 ft gain). Day 2: Bachelor Flats to Dome-Chickamin Col base camp (3.2 miles, 2,600 ft gain). Day 3: Climb East Face of Middle Gunsight (4-6 hours climbing time, 600 ft gain) and descend to base camp (3-4 hours). Day 4: Return to Bachelor Flats (5-6 hours). Day 5: Return to trailhead (6 miles, 4,500 ft loss).

name: East Face
approach: Access via SR-20 north of Cascade Loop; drive past the hairpin turn just east of Washington Pass to the pullout near Milepost 166 on the south side of the highway. A climbers trail drops from the pullout, immediately crosses Early Winters Creek, and ascends steeply through timbered terrain to a bench camp around 6,500 feet. From camp, continue east toward the Wine Spires. From the bench camp, traverse to approach Chablis Spire via Burgundy Col approach (recommended spring-fall; 2-5 hours total from trailhead) or via Silver Star Creek drainage (recommended for winter; approach in snow). Chablis is reached after traversing past or over Burgundy Col area.
descent: Downclimb carefully to locate the large horn anchor with existing slings. Execute two double-rope rappels with 60m ropes: first rappel to intermediate anchor, second rappel completes descent to the base of the East Face.

bivy.name: Burgundy Col high camp — west side, the Wine Spires
bivy.notes: The narrow saddle between Burgundy Spire and the ridge, and the standard high camp for the Wine Spires and for the Silver Star Glacier approached from the highway side. Published elevations disagree by a couple of hundred feet, with figures from roughly 7,720 to 7,950 in circulation, so treat any single number as approximate. It is exposed to wind from both sides and several parties have dropped back down the west slope to sleep after a rough night. Camping here removes about 1,500 ft of the scree from summit day, which is most of the argument for carrying overnight gear up it.
bivy.water: No spring or stream. Parties melt snow from the lingering patches on the glacier side of the col, which normally hold into late summer but can be rock-hard in the morning or gone entirely in a dry, late season. Many simply haul all their water up the scree, which is the single heaviest decision on this approach.
bivy.permit: None. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit, unlike the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
bivy.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

bivy.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — west side
bivy.notes: The flat, sheltered alternative to sleeping at the col, in trees before the timbered rib gives way to open scree. Reports consistently call it the more pleasant camp of the two, at the cost of extra vertical on summit morning. Elevation is quoted anywhere from about 6,400 to 6,500 ft depending on which flat spot a party used. Its value is almost entirely the spring: if that has failed, the bench loses most of its advantage over the col.
bivy.water: The most dependable water on this approach, but NOT from the obvious place. The creek shown on maps immediately east of the bench is frequently dry, while a spring roughly ten minutes north of camp keeps running well into September in most years. Confirm it before committing, and expect insects around it.
bivy.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, non-wilderness, so no permit or reservation applies.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots on a wooded bench, with a large boulder and an old fire ring as the usual landmark; comfortably three or four tents

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
bivy.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
bivy.water: No drinking water at the campground. Early Winters Creek runs alongside and needs filtering; Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds, farther east, have drinking water in season.
bivy.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
bivy.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles

bivy.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — west side
bivy.notes: Not an established campsite so much as a fallback for a party that has run out of daylight or water partway up the talus. The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.
bivy.water: Genuinely unreliable and conditions-dependent. At least one party found a trickle running here in a season when the bench camp creek below was dry, which makes it worth checking on the way up, but nothing about it is dependable enough to plan a camp around.
bivy.permit: None. Non-wilderness National Forest land; no permit, quota or registration.
bivy.capacity: Improvised, one or two small parties at most; flat ground has to be found or built rather than chosen

itinerary: Day 1: Early departure from trailhead at Milepost 166 (~6am). Hike to bench camp at 6,500 feet (2-4 hours). Establish camp, rest, hydrate, prepare for next day. Day 2: Early alpine start from camp toward Chablis Spire via Burgundy Col or direct approach (1.5-2 hours to base). 4-pitch climb and summit (3-4 hours). Descent via 2 rappels (1-1.5 hours). Return to camp. Day 3: Pack out, return to trailhead via hiking trail (2-4 hours downhill).

name: East Face
approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to Burlington/Sedro-Woolley, then east on SR-20 through Marblemount and over Rainy Pass to Washington Pass; from Winthrop/Mazama it's a quick 20-30 minute drive west on SR-20 instead. Park beside the small pond on SR-20 a few hundred yards east of Washington Pass (about 5,400 ft). Walk around the pond's left side and take the climbers' path into the forest, heading roughly south-southwest; it comes out onto talus beneath the east walls of Liberty Bell and Minuteman near 6,000 ft. Work up the talus to Minuteman's lower left corner, around 6,600 ft. Plan on about an hour and roughly 1,200 ft of climbing from the car.
descent: About 3 rappels with a single 60m rope back to the approach talus.

bivy.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside bivy
bivy.notes: The usual answer for a car-to-car day on this group, and the start of every west-side approach, about a mile west of Washington Pass. Parties routinely sleep at the lot or at the highway hairpin rather than walking in, because the approaches are short enough that a high camp buys little. There are no facilities and no water; it is a place to sleep in or beside the car, not a campsite. Highway 20 is closed through the winter, so this is unavailable until the road reopens.
bivy.water: None at the trailhead. Carry what you need.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park
bivy.capacity: Informal, at the parking area — no prepared sites

bivy.name: Liberty Bell basin dispersed sites
bivy.notes: Sites in the basin on the west side of the group, reached by following the Blue Lake trail and then the signed climbers' path that branches off it toward the group. Worth it if you want to be under the west-side routes at first light rather than walking up from the road. Note the separate restriction around Blue Lake itself, where overnight camping is not allowed within a quarter mile of the lake — the basin sites are the ones to aim for, not the lakeshore. Treat it as a basin camp below the spires rather than a fixed spot.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and seasonal runoff in the basin — unreliable once the snow has gone
bivy.permit: No permit for dispersed camping; this is national forest, not the national park
bivy.capacity: Scattered dispersed sites, small parties

itinerary: Typically done as a single long day from a car camp or bivy near Washington Pass: early start, a 45-minute-to-1-hour approach, roughly 6 pitches of technical climbing, then a 3-rappel descent back to the approach talus and the same trail out. No bivy on the route itself is standard.

name: East Ridge
approach: From the Reflection Lakes trailhead, follow the maintained Pinnacle Saddle Trail 1.3 mi (~1,000-1,050 ft gain) to the Pinnacle-Plummer saddle. From the saddle, continue on the unmaintained boot path east/behind Pinnacle toward Castle Peak to reach the Castle-Pinnacle col; the east ridge of Pinnacle rises directly from this col. Allow roughly 2-3 hours and about 1,500 ft of gain for this approach segment.
descent: Rappel the south face from the pitch-2 anchor (confirm your rope reaches a stance first), or continue over the true summit and descend via the Southwest Scramble gully back to the saddle.

bivy.name: Cougar Rock Campground
bivy.notes: For a Tatoosh trip this is the practical drive-in base, sitting between Longmire and the switchbacks up to Narada Falls and Reflection Lakes, so the morning drive to any of these trailheads is short. It runs roughly late May into early autumn and is closed the rest of the year — which puts it out of reach for exactly the season the Lane Peak gullies are in. Book it if you want a bed for a Pinnacle or Unicorn day climb without dealing with the wilderness permit system at all.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground; no hookups at any site
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — a developed campground. Reservations through Recreation.gov during the summer peak. Park entrance fee applies separately, and the park has used timed-entry reservations for the Nisqually/Paradise corridor in recent summers, which can affect what time you can drive up.
bivy.capacity: Around 173 individual sites plus 5 group sites

bivy.name: Reflection Lakes area winter snow camp
bivy.notes: The base people reach for when Stevens Canyon Road is gated and Lane Peak or Pinnacle is the objective, since it puts you at the top of the road walk rather than the bottom. In practice most parties skip it: the Zipper and Lover's Lane, and Pinnacle and The Castle in winter dress, are routinely done car-to-car from the Narada Falls lot, and the honest variable on those routes is the approach and the snow stability, not where you slept. The reason to camp is the gate — the road above Longmire is closed overnight and reopens on a morning schedule, so a dawn start from a car is not available the way it is elsewhere. Habituated foxes here have a long record of working over unattended food.
bivy.water: None liquid in winter — melt snow
bivy.permit: Winter wilderness permit, obtained in person at Longmire rather than online. Camping on snow is broadly allowed once the pack is deep enough, which the park sets at roughly two feet for the Reflection Lakes and Mazama Ridge side and five feet at Paradise itself. Blue bags for waste; food hung or in a hard-sided container.
bivy.capacity: Parties up to 12; anything larger is directed to the designated Paradise group area

itinerary: Full alpine day: trailhead to Castle-Pinnacle col (~2-3 hr), roped climbing to the summit (~2 hr for the three pitches), summit break, then descent (~3 hr) — commonly a 7-8 hour car-to-car day, longer if combined with The Castle.

waypoints.name: Reflection Lakes area winter snow camp

name: North Buttress (Thread of Gneiss)
approach: From the Lower Goodell Creek trailhead, day one covers more than six miles and 6,000 feet of elevation gain to a col near the Chopping Block. Day two crosses snow, slabs, and talus through Crescent Creek Basin, then crampons up to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col, followed by one rappel down onto the Mustard Glacier to reach the base of the North Buttress.
itinerary: Day 1: Lower Goodell Creek TH to a col near the Chopping Block (~6+ mi, ~6,000 ft gain). Day 2: traverse Crescent Creek Basin, cross to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col, rappel onto the Mustard Glacier, then climb the North Buttress (9 pitches, 5.9, ~2,000 ft).

name: East Wilmans Spire
approach: From Granite Falls, drive the paved Mountain Loop Highway east roughly 31 miles (passing the Verlot Public Service Center) to Barlow Pass, where pavement ends and the Monte Cristo Road is gated to motor vehicles. Hike or mountain-bike the flat, gated road about 4 miles along the South Fork Sauk River to the historic Monte Cristo townsite (a washout near the Twin Bridges area may require a ford or log crossing of the river). From the townsite, pick up the Glacier Basin Trail and follow it a short distance before leaving the trail to climb a steep talus/scree gully - snow-covered and firmer in early season, loose and increasingly rockfall-prone once melted out by mid/late summer - up to the east notch/col below East Wilmans Spire, where the roped climbing begins.
descent: Two single-rope rappels to the top of pitch 1, then climb back over the short 5.5 crack (or make a third rappel) to the east notch, and downclimb the approach gully.

bivy.name: Glacier Basin — Ray's Knoll and Mystery Hill
bivy.notes: This is the working high camp for the northern half of the group. Cadet forms the basin's north arc and Monte Cristo Peak the southeast arc, so both go as reasonable summit days from here rather than the brutal round trips they are from the road. Foggy Peak rises straight out of the ground immediately northeast of the townsite and is climbed off this same trail, and the Wilmans Peaks and the Spires are reached by leaving the Glacier Basin trail low and working up towards the '76 Glacier side. Getting here means the four-mile road walk to the townsite, then the trail past the cabins and over 76 Creek, half a mile of old road grade along Glacier Creek, then a long steep stretch beside Glacier Falls that is more slick rock scramble than trail and is genuinely unpleasant wet or iced. Snow holds in the basin into July most years and the falls section is the part that turns parties around early season. The whole basin is old mining ground, so stay on the established pads and off the thin heather.
bivy.water: Carry it in. Surface water through this basin and the drainage below has been measured with arsenic and other heavy metals above drinking water standards, and filtering, boiling and chemical treatment remove none of that. Snowmelt high in the basin, well away from old workings and tailings, is the least bad option if you run dry, and it is not a plan to rely on.
bivy.permit: Inside the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness — free self-issue wilderness permit from the trailhead box, no quota or reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Barlow Pass. Campfires are prohibited in Glacier Basin and within a quarter mile of the trail; carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: Moderate — established pockets on the timbered knoll in the middle of the basin and on the rise beyond it, enough for several parties spread out, but they are the only durable ground and they fill on a fine weekend

bivy.name: Monte Cristo townsite campground, four miles up the closed road
bivy.notes: Because the road is gated at Barlow Pass, staging here is the normal plan for this group rather than a luxury: it turns a four-mile approach walk into an evening stroll and puts Glacier Basin, Poodle Dog Pass and every summit above them within a sane day. The walk in follows the old road and railway grade with almost no gain, and it is flat enough that many parties ride bikes and stash them at the townsite. About a mile up, the old road bridge over the South Fork Sauk is long gone; the crossing is on logs or a ford, and it is the one piece of the approach that varies year to year and can be genuinely serious in snowmelt or after heavy rain. Beyond it the timber road bridges over the creek gullies are intact. The ground here was remediated after the tailings and mine debris were found to be badly contaminated, and that cleanup is why the area is open at all, but old workings, adits and metal remain scattered off the paths. Access is seasonal at the margins: Barlow Pass is at the end of the pavement and stays reachable from Granite Falls when the gravel stretch of the loop towards Bedal is gated shut for winter.
bivy.water: Do not drink the local water. The South Fork Sauk and the creeks around the townsite carry arsenic and heavy metals from a century of mining and milling, at levels above drinking water standards, and a backcountry filter or a rolling boil deals with the biology and leaves the metals exactly where they were. Bring every litre you intend to drink, for the stay and for the walk out.
bivy.permit: The campground and townsite flat sit outside designated wilderness, so no wilderness permit is needed to sleep here and fires are allowed in the provided rings; the boundary is crossed a short way up either the Glacier Basin or the Poodle Dog trail, where the free self-issue permit applies. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass at Barlow Pass. Much of the townsite is private land — roughly half the original lots are still in private hands with inherited mining rights, cabins are posted no trespassing, and some are occupied. Camp only in the marked sites and treat everything else as somebody's property.
bivy.capacity: Small — roughly six developed walk-in sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet on the flat by the old townsite, plus a scatter of informal spots along the road grade coming in

bivy.name: Barlow Pass roadhead
bivy.notes: Sleeping at the car is what most parties actually do the night before a long single push into this group, because the four-mile road walk to the townsite is flat and fast enough to be swallowed by a pre-dawn start. It is the last point vehicles reach: the gate closes the Monte Cristo road here, and it is also where the Weden Creek trail towards Gothic Basin and Del Campo branches off a mile up the road, so the same parking serves objectives that have nothing else in common. Break-ins at a busy roadhead are a known problem, so leave nothing visible. Nothing here has any shelter and there is no reason to linger; treat it as a staging point rather than a night out, and if you want a real camp, walk the four miles in.
bivy.water: None. Nothing potable here and nothing potable anywhere up the road, so this is where you load every litre for the trip.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to leave a vehicle. No wilderness permit needed at the pass itself, but pick up the free self-issue permit here for anything crossing into the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness above the townsite.
bivy.capacity: Car bivy only — a gravel parking area at the gate, no sites, no tables, no pads. It fills on summer weekends and it is not a campground.

itinerary: Car-to-car is feasible in a long day for a fit, fast party (biking the Monte Cristo road saves significant time and energy), but many parties break the roughly 4,000 ft of total elevation gain into an overnight at Glacier Basin, climbing East Wilmans Spire the following morning and hiking/biking back out to Barlow Pass the same day.

waypoints.name: Monte Cristo townsite campground, four miles up the closed road

name: Easy Getaway
approach: This is a distinct approach from the one used for Cutthroat Peak, which starts from an unmarked highway pullout about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass with no maintained trail. For Cutthroat Wall, start on the maintained Cutthroat Creek Trail #483 from the Cutthroat Trailhead kiosk. After a short distance on the main trail, leave it via a cairned path that cuts into the forest, then follow cairns and a climbers' path (roughly 1.5-2 miles, 45 min-2 hrs total) through brush and talus, trending toward the buttress, to reach the base of Cutthroat Wall.
descent: Shared Cutthroat Wall descent: one rappel from the notch to a ramp (two 60m ropes; a single 60m can fall short), then an ascending gully/ledge system on skier's left back to the base - study the beta carefully, as it's easy to get wrong.

bivy.name: Cutthroat Creek trailhead
bivy.notes: The lot sits a mile up the forest road from SR 20 and has a vault toilet but no water. It is the start for Cutthroat Wall and for the Cutthroat Lake trail toward Cutthroat Pass, and some parties sleep here or in a pullout on the road in before a pre-dawn start, though the lot itself is signed for day use and how strictly that is read varies; dispersed camping in the trees along the forest road below is the uncontroversial option. Access is entirely gated by the SR 20 winter closure, and the road has been shut for construction windows in recent seasons, so confirm before driving out.
bivy.water: None — no potable water at the trailhead. Cutthroat Creek runs below the lot and needs filtering.
bivy.permit: No camping permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day pass covers parking. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, NOT the national park, so there is no backcountry permit system here at all.
bivy.capacity: Large gravel lot, roughly 20-30 vehicles; fills on summer weekends with larch-season hikers

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground to Washington Pass, on SR 20 along Early Winters Creek six or seven miles east of the pass, just past the turn for the Cutthroat Creek road. Because nothing here can be booked, arriving Friday evening in July or August is a gamble and the fallback is dispersed camping on a spur road. The season runs roughly May or June through September or October, entirely dependent on when the highway opens and when snow returns.
bivy.water: No drinking water at Lone Fir. Early Winters Creek runs through the campground and needs filtering; Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds, farther east, have drinking water in season.
bivy.permit: No reservations and no permit — first-come, first-served with a nightly fee. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to camp, only to park at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: 27 sites, tents and small RVs

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby
bivy.notes: Klipchuck sits about a quarter mile off SR 20 in fir and pine down-valley toward Mazama, low enough to be warm and dry when the passes are still wet. Early Winters Campground is further east, smaller at around a dozen tent sites, split by the highway near the Methow River, and fills quickly. Both are a longer drive to the trailhead than Lone Fir, which is the tradeoff for a better chance of finding a site on a busy weekend.
bivy.water: Drinking water spigots in season; vault toilets. Water is turned off at the end of the season while the sites stay usable.
bivy.permit: First-come, first-served, nightly fee, no reservation and no permit required.
bivy.capacity: 46 sites, the largest campground on this stretch of highway

bivy.name: Cutthroat Wall base terrace
bivy.notes: The approach leaves the old roadbed a quarter mile from the trailhead at cairns, then climbs left through trees and light brush to a flat bench beneath the west-northwest-facing granite. Most parties do these routes car-to-car in a day, so a bivy here is for a late start or a two-day plan rather than standard practice. The wall faces away from morning sun, which makes an early camp less useful than it looks on the map. The crag is sometimes catalogued under Little Liberty Bell, which is the same approach and the same ground.
bivy.water: No water on the terrace itself. Fill in Cutthroat Creek low on the approach and carry it up.
bivy.permit: None — dispersed national forest camping, no permit and no quota.
bivy.capacity: A small flat area under the cliff; room for one or two parties at most

itinerary: Plan a long car-to-car day: pre-dawn start, 1-2 hr approach/bushwhack to base, roughly 6-8 hrs for the 8 pitches, then 1-2 hrs to descend. Budget a full daylight window given the approach and loose descent.

waypoints.name: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby

name: North Ridge
approach: Same approach as the East Ridge to high camp on the Inspiration Glacier, then cross the Inspiration Glacier around the east end of the East Ridge and traverse the glacier on the mountain's north side at about 8,100 ft to the NW Ice Couloir notch at the base of the North Ridge.
descent: Reverse the North Ridge back to the notch and down to camp, or finish via the East Ridge and descend that way.

bivy.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
bivy.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

bivy.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
bivy.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
bivy.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

bivy.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
bivy.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
bivy.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
bivy.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
bivy.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

bivy.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
bivy.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
bivy.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

bivy.name: Eldorado Basin camp
bivy.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
bivy.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A bear canister is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
bivy.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

bivy.name: Eldorado (East Ridge) camp

itinerary: Day 1: Approach to high camp. Day 2: Descend to the North Ridge base, climb the ridge (roughly a half-day, ~5 hrs round trip from camp), descend, hike out or camp a third night.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek / Cascade River Road TH

name: West Arete
approach: Start at the Eldorado Creek trailhead on Cascade River Road, follow the climbers' trail up Eldorado Creek into the Roush Creek basin, camp near the base of the East Ridge (about 7,500 ft), then cross the Inspiration and McAllister glaciers to Dorado Needle Col and make a loose fourth-class downclimb into the Marble Creek cirque, traversing to the toe of the arete near 6,000 ft. Typically a 3-day trip (approach day, climb day, exit day); the first roughly 800 ft of climbing is Class 4 before harder 5th-class sections.
descent: Descend via Eldorado's East Ridge route back toward the high camp.

itinerary: Day 1: Approach via Eldorado Creek/Roush Creek/Eldorado Glacier to a high camp near the East Ridge base (~7,400 ft). Day 2: Continue via Dorado Col to the base of the west face and climb the ~19-pitch, ~2,800-3,000 ft arête (5.6-5.8) to the summit, then descend via the East Ridge back to camp — a long day, historically up to ~17 hours round-trip from camp. Day 3: Hike out to the trailhead.

name: Elephant Butte Standard Route (Stetattle/Sourdough Ridge)
approach: Drive State Route 20 (North Cascades Highway) to milepost 126 and turn off at the sign for the village of Diablo, a Seattle City Light company town. Park near the river across from the domed swimming pool; the Sourdough Mountain Trail begins immediately behind the pool building (roughly 890-900 ft). Follow the trail as it switchbacks steeply through forest. At an unmarked junction around 4,300-4,400 ft, leave the maintained trail and head up onto the open crest of Sourdough/Stetattle Ridge (roughly 6,500 ft) rather than continuing to the Sourdough Mountain Lookout; if you reach the Sourdough Creek crossing and open views of Diablo Lake, you have gone past the turn-off. From the ridge crest, continue along the mostly open, trail-less ridge toward Elephant Butte.
descent: Reverse the ascent: back along Sourdough/Stetattle Ridge to the unmarked trail junction, then down the Sourdough Mountain Trail to Diablo.

bivy.name: Sourdough Camp, Sourdough Creek
bivy.notes: A little over four miles up from Diablo, this is the only designated camp on the lower half of the approach and it exists mainly to break a brutal climb. The Sourdough Mountain trail gains close to five thousand feet in a bit over five miles and is routinely called the hardest maintained trail in the park; the first three and a half miles are relentless forest switchbacks with nothing to drink. Stopping here makes the second day the good one. Note that the climbers' line for Elephant Butte does not continue to the lookout at all — it leaves this trail at an unmarked junction somewhere around four thousand three hundred to four thousand four hundred feet and turns north up the ridge crest west of the creek. No elevation is recorded for the camp because no confident figure was found. Both this camp and the trail it sits on have been closed by fire for most of the last three years; confirm before planning around it.
bivy.water: Sourdough Creek runs at the camp and is the first water on the whole climb from Diablo — the lower trail has essentially none. Early in the season the crossing can be bridged by snow, which is worth treating with care rather than walking onto.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, collected at the Marblemount wilderness office or through the park's issuing process. This is a designated camp assigned by night rather than open ground, so a walk-up can be refused. A bear canister is required here through the main season; the park lends them free at the permit desk. No fires. Pets are not allowed at the camp.
bivy.capacity: A few tent spots only, with a hard limit of four people on the site. That is the smallest party cap of anything on this approach and it rules the camp out for a larger group entirely.

bivy.name: Sourdough Mountain summit ground
bivy.notes: The summit sits a little over six thousand feet directly above Diablo Lake, and parties heading out along the ridge in snow conditions have used it as a first night. It is included because the road to Diablo is west of the seasonal highway gate and therefore open all year, which makes this one of the few high camps in the corridor reachable in winter — a late-March overnight on continuous snow is a known way to do the ridge, with the caveat that spring sun softens the slopes badly by mid-morning. For a summer ascent of the butte it is a detour, since the climbers' line leaves the trail well below the lookout and never comes here. It also carries the same warning as everything else: the trail, both designated camps, and the Sourdough and Elephant Butte zones have all been closed by an active fire in the drainage, on top of an earlier fire that shut the trail for two and a half years before it briefly reopened. Check the closure status first; it is the single thing most likely to end this trip.
bivy.water: Melted snow in the cold months, which is when this site makes sense. In summer there is nothing at the summit and the tarns further along the ridge are the supply.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit for the Sourdough cross-country zone: six people per party, six parties a night, walk-up only. The lookout building is closed and camping is not permitted at it, so the site is the open ground near the top rather than the structure. Same durable-surface, no-fire and no-meadow rules as the rest of the zone.
bivy.capacity: Open ground near the summit, a small party at a time. In winter and spring it is a snow camp with no defined pitch at all.

bivy.name: Stetattle Ridge tarn camps
bivy.notes: This is the camp for the peak. Once the climbers' line breaks out of the trees near six thousand feet the ridge runs north-west in a long open crest of heather, gravel and tarns, and parties simply pick a spot. The best-documented ascent camped beside a late-season tarn at about six and a half thousand feet and went for the summit from there. It is still a long way: from the ridge high point the ground drops something like fifteen hundred feet before you regain that and another thousand to the top, and a full trip is closer to twenty miles and ten thousand feet of gain and loss over two nights. Several strong parties have reached the ridge in a single push and turned round because the butte was still too far. The north-east side of the crest is very steep, so stay on it or just south-west of it. Snow-free is roughly late July into September, which is unhelpfully the same window in which the water disappears.
bivy.water: Small tarns and snowmelt ponds scattered over the ridge — plentiful in late June, and the single best reason to come early. They do dry. By August in a warm year parties report water on the ridge becoming a real problem, and which pools survive latest is not documented anywhere reliable. Late in the season carry enough to camp dry.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required. There is no Stetattle Ridge zone — the ridge falls between the Sourdough zone and the Elephant Butte zone, and your permit has to name the one you will actually sleep in. Both allow a party of six and six parties a night. Neither is reservable in advance: they are walk-up zones, issued in person, with a share of the allocation held for same-day and next-day pickup. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground, never in the meadow pockets that make the ridge look inviting, and not within a hundred feet of a tarn. No fires in a cross-country zone. Waste in a cathole, or carried out on snow and bare rock. A canister is not formally required in these two zones, but the ridge is open ground with nothing to hang from, so bring one anyway.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed cross-country ground rather than sites. Small grassy pockets and gravel benches recur the length of the ridge, easily enough for the zone's limit of six parties, and no two accounts stop in the same place.

bivy.name: Improvised camp on the shoulder of Elephant Butte
bivy.notes: There is no camp at the base of this peak and inventing one would be dishonest — parties sleep where the daylight runs out, on whatever flat ground the shoulder offers. From the ridge the summit itself is not technical, more a broad lump on a crest than a spire, and the standard finish takes its gentle west side at walking-to-scrambling ground. The east ridge is a different proposition entirely and has been described by a party crossing it on a long Picket traverse as among the hardest ground of that whole trip, needing roped downclimbs and rappels — so do not read the easy summit as an easy mountain from every side. The named benches near the pass east of the butte belong to the traverse route rather than to this approach, and a party coming from Stetattle Ridge will not pass them. No elevation is recorded: no account that slept on this shoulder coming from Stetattle Ridge stated one, and the figures published for the traverse-side benches describe different ground.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small pools, entirely seasonal. There is no dependable source and nothing to plan on. Fill on the ridge before committing to the descent toward the butte.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit for the Elephant Butte cross-country zone: six people maximum, six parties a night, walk-up only from Marblemount. Zone camping legally begins a mile from any designated camp and half a mile from any trail and out of sight of both, which up here is automatic. Durable surfaces only, no fires, waste packed out above treeline.
bivy.capacity: No established site and no name. Parties travelling the crest report finding flat ground on the shoulder and on the benches near the pass east of the peak, tight enough that three tents felt crowded. Treat it as somewhere you stop, not somewhere you book.

itinerary: As a dedicated objective: Day 1 — drive to Diablo, hike the Sourdough Mountain Trail and ridge to a camp near Sourdough/Stetattle Ridge; Day 2 — continue the ridge traverse to Elephant Butte's summit and return. A fit, light party can also do the full round trip from Diablo in one very long day. As an approach leg into the Southern Pickets, most parties budget two to three days from Diablo to reach Elephant Butte with full overnight packs before continuing into the range.

name: Ellation
approach: From I-5 Exit 255, drive SR-542 (Mt. Baker Highway) east about 46 miles, then turn left onto Forest Road 32 (Hannegan Pass Road) and follow it about 5.3 miles to the road-end Hannegan Pass Trailhead. Mamie Peak's tiered granite walls stand directly above. Walk the Hannegan Pass Trail a few minutes to a clearing below a large white boulder perched high on the slope, then leave the trail on a faint, brushy climbers' path up a gully, a dry creekbed and steep woods to the base of the wall: about an hour and 1,200 ft of gain.
descent: Rappel the route: 8 single-rope (70m) raps from bolted/fixed anchors back to the base.

bivy.name: Hannegan trailhead, end of the Ruth Creek road
bivy.notes: This is where nearly every trip in the zone starts, and it is the answer for a party that drives out after work and wants a short night before an alpine start on Ruth. It is also the base for Mount Sefrit, which is normally done car-to-car from a pullout a few miles back down the road and has no camp of its own worth listing. Road access has been the weak link: a washout near the end of FS 32 cut vehicle access to the sites at the road end for a period, a bypass has since been built above the damaged section, and both the road and the trailhead have a history of being reachable in one season and not the next. Confirm the road is open to the end before committing to the drive out. In winter and spring the road beyond the Goat Mountain trailhead runs under avalanche terrain and the last miles are usually snowbound well into spring.
bivy.water: Ruth Creek runs below the road and is easy to reach, and side streams cross the lower trail. Reliable all season, but it is glacial and forest runoff — filter rather than just treating.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park; a Washington state Discover Pass does NOT work at a Forest Service fee site. No overnight backcountry permit is needed to sleep here or anywhere between the road and the pass, though a free self-issue wilderness registration at the trailhead is the norm once you walk in. Fires are subject to seasonal restrictions and are worth checking against the current burn ban rather than assumed.
bivy.capacity: A small set of rough roadside sites at the road end plus informal pullouts along the last miles; a handful of parties, and the parking area fills on summer weekends

itinerary: A single long day: hike in (~1 hr), climb the 8 pitches, rappel the route back to the base (8 raps), then hike out. Not typically climbed as a multi-day or bivy objective.

name: Ellen Pea
approach: M&M Wall, also known as Supercave Wall for the tennis-court-sized cave crossing the cliff at mid-height, is one of the largest roadside walls at Washington Pass. Park at a pullout near milepost 166 on SR-20, about 3 miles east of the hairpin turns below Washington Pass. From the highway, head directly uphill (west, away from the creek) toward the talus at the base of the Supercave gully, following it up and briefly left before rejoining the gully; it takes roughly 1 hour to reach the lower ledge and about 1 hour 10 minutes to reach the upper ledge and base of the longer routes.
descent: Descend via established descent route, using rappels and downclimbing as necessary. Multiple anchor points and protection required. Route-finding is critical in poor visibility.

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: This is the honest answer for most objectives here: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

itinerary: Single long day from the car: roughly 1–1.2 hour approach, 7 pitches of climbing, then rappel the route with two ropes to the base and descend the gully to the car.

name: Enchantment Enchainment
approach: From the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road, follow the Stuart Lake trail up Mountaineer Creek through old burn toward Stuart Lake. Beyond the lake leave the trail and climb the slopes, then steep snow, to the notch on Stuart's northwest face that gives the shortcut onto the upper West Ridge. The West Ridge is normally approached from the south, so this north-side access sees little traffic; expect snow in the notch and gully well into summer.
itinerary: Most parties take two or three days, and the Enchantment overnight permit decides how. Without a lottery permit nobody may camp inside the permit zone (Stuart Lake, Colchuck Lake, the Core and the rest of the zone), so an unpermitted party must either do the whole loop in a single push or split it into separate day trips from the Stuart Lake trailhead, for example Stuart, Sherpa and Argonaut on one day, then Colchuck, Dragontail, Little Annapurna, McClellan, Enchantment Peak and Cannon on another. With an overnight permit, a common split is Stuart, Sherpa and Argonaut on day one with a camp in the permitted zone (Colchuck Lake or the Core), then the Colchuck-Dragontail col and the Core summits over the next one or two days before exiting.

name: East Ridge (Prusik Pass)
approach: Reach Prusik Pass either from the west (Stuart Lake TH -> Colchuck Lake -> Aasgard Pass -> across the core Enchantment basin) or from the north/east via the longer Snow Creek/Snow Lakes trail (FST 1553) and the upper basin. From Prusik Pass, head west onto Enchantment Peak's east ridge.
descent: Reverse the ridge back to Prusik Pass, then retrace whichever approach was used (Aasgard Pass or Snow Lakes).
itinerary: Commonly combined with Prusik Peak, Little Annapurna, and/or McClellan Peak in a single long day or overnight from a basin camp, since all stage from the same Prusik Pass/core basin area.

name: Fantasy Falls
approach: Drive Stevens Canyon Road to the Bench Lake/Snow Lake trailhead, on the south side of the road about 1.5 miles east of the Reflection Lakes parking area and roughly 3 miles beyond Narada Falls. From the trailhead at about 4,550 ft, follow the Bench Lake/Snow Lake trail 0.75 mile to Bench Lake, then a further 0.5 mile to Snow Lake at 4,685 ft, which sits in a glacial cirque directly below Unicorn Peak. From the lake, continue up the Unicorn Creek drainage south and east into the upper cirque to the base of the northwest face. Total is roughly 1.5-2 miles and about 1,500 ft of gain from the car to the base of the ice. In winter, when Stevens Canyon Road is gated, add about 3 miles of unplowed road from Narada Falls; one spring party on skis reported four hours from the car to the base of the climbing.
descent: Top out on the summit and reverse the standard route: one short rappel off the summit block, then down the class 3 south slope to the 6,605 ft west col and back into the basin.
itinerary: Realistically a long single push in winter, or a two-day trip if you want to climb the ice with a rested party. Single push: leave the plowed Longmire-Paradise road near Narada Falls very early (2-4 a.m.), ski or snowshoe the ~3 miles of gated Stevens Canyon Road to the Bench Lake/Snow Lake trailhead, continue past Bench Lake to Snow Lake and up Unicorn Creek into the cirque, and be racking up at the base of the face around first light — figure roughly four hours car to base. Climb the three pitches to the summit, rappel the summit block and descend the south slope to the 6,605 ft col, then reverse the basin, gully and trail to the road, and ski the road back out. Two-day version: camp at Snow Lake (two designated wilderness sites, bear pole and toilet, wilderness permit required) or bivy higher in the cirque, climb the route the following morning with a short approach, and walk out the same day.

name: First Amendment
approach: From the pullout, an unmarked but well-worn climbers' trail drops steeply from the west/southwest end of the turnout through loose dirt and rock into the trees, marked intermittently by cairns. The path crosses Early Winters Creek (on logs) before climbing into an open rocky drainage/talus below the formation; the final approach to the base involves loose 3rd/4th-class slabs, with sandy access ledges and a fixed rope on parts of the standard line.
descent: Descend via Spontaneity Arete's rappel line or gully option after joining that route near the top.

bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
