bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

itinerary: Early start given the length (9 pitches, ~900 ft) and remote approach; expect a full, long alpine day combining the shared approach, traverse to the base, the technical pitches, and a Spontaneity-Arête-style descent.

waypoints.name: SR-20 turnout below Le Petit Cheval (east of Washington Pass)

name: Flight of the Falcon
approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to the Arlington exit, then SR 530 east through Oso to Darrington, and turn onto Squire Creek Road at the west end of town, following it to the parking area where it's gated off by washout damage. From there the approach is long and rough: hike the old roadbed past a landslide crossing (~5 minutes in), reach the original road end around 30-40 minutes from the car, then follow a faint trail through a dry streambed and alder brush, ford Squire Creek, and pick through obscure forest track before finally breaking out into the open basin roughly 2 hours from the car. The route is still far above: climb the bolted 5.8 slab and the dirty low-fifth crack to the foot of Roan Wall, scramble up its left side to the saddle where Salish Peak comes into view, and cross the high basin to the toe of the south face, about 6 hours from the car in all. This is a known bushwhacky, unmaintained approach typical of Darrington-area crags, with route-finding (flagging, cairns) required in several spots.
descent: Rappel from the top of Pitch 7 with 2x60m ropes, or climb to the true summit and walk off left/west.

bivy.name: Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac
bivy.notes: The Squire Creek road out of the west end of old Darrington has been cut by a washout well short of its historic end for many years, so the drivable road end is A moving target and the walk in to Squire Creek Wall is longer than older descriptions suggest. Parties sleeping in the car or under a tarp at the closure are doing so to get an early start on that extra walking, not because there is anything established there. Confirm the current closure point before committing — how far you can drive has changed repeatedly between seasons, and it is the single biggest variable in a Squire Creek Wall day.
bivy.water: Squire Creek runs close by and is dependable, but needs treating
bivy.permit: None for dispersed camping on forest land; the usual 14-day and setback rules apply.
bivy.capacity: A few parties, informal

bivy.name: Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County
bivy.notes: Sits in old-growth timber near where Squire Creek meets the North Fork Stillaguamish, a few miles west of Darrington on SR 530 — not on the Mountain Loop Highway, and not up the Squire Creek road itself. It is the most comfortable base for a weekend on the Darrington granite, with flush toilets and a swimmable creek, at the cost of a drive back into town each morning. Because it is county-run rather than Forest Service, the fee schedule, season and reservation window are set separately from the national forest campgrounds and should be checked on their own.
bivy.water: Piped drinking water via spigots through the campground; reliable in season
bivy.permit: None — this is a county park, not Forest Service. Nightly fee, reservations through the Snohomish County Parks system. A Northwest Forest Pass does nothing here.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 30 non-hookup sites, tents and RVs, reservable

itinerary: Given the 6+ hour approach, parties typically either commit to a single very-early (pre-dawn) push (one reported round trip was about 17 hours 50 minutes car-to-car), or hike in during the afternoon/evening and bivy at Martha's Place boulder near the head of the basin, climbing the route the next day and hiking out — splitting the long round trip across two days.

name: Southwest Slope (Standard Route)
approach: From Chelan, take the Lady of the Lake ferry (or a floatplane) to Stehekin Landing. Ride the NPS shuttle bus 4.4 miles up Stehekin Valley Road to Harlequin Bridge ($5 fare), cross the bridge, and follow the road past Harlequin Camp and the Stehekin Airport to pick up the Stehekin River Trail. Follow this mostly flat trail southeastward about 3 miles to the signed Devore Creek Trail junction. The Devore Creek Trail then climbs steeply through rock bluffs and open forest for about 1 mile, enters the Glacier Peak Wilderness, and traverses brushy, dry hillside for roughly 3 more miles to Bird Creek Camp (4,200 ft) — the only designated camp in the area, with room for about three tents. From Bird Creek Camp, most parties do Flora as a long day round trip: bushwhack through open forest (spiderwebs, chest-high brush, and blowdown reported) toward the saddle south of Enigma Peak, then follow the route description above to the summit.
descent: Reverse the ascent line down the southwest talus/scree to the Enigma Peak saddle and back to Bird Creek Camp.

bivy.name: Bird Creek Camp
bivy.notes: The only designated camp on the upper Devore Creek trail, just before the Bird Creek crossing. Parties base here and climb Flora in a long day, 4 to 5 hours up. Higher camps are possible in the larch basin around 6,500 to 6,900 ft.
bivy.water: Bird Creek, beside camp
bivy.permit: Same overnight permit as the rest of the trip
bivy.capacity: About three tents and a cook area

bivy.name: Purple Point and Harlequin — the landing camps, and the boat that decides the trip
bivy.notes: Read this before any other site in the zone. Stehekin has no road to it. The only practical way in is the scheduled passenger boat up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, and the timetable, not your fitness, sets the shape of the trip. The slow boat takes roughly four hours each way and the express about two and a half; a typical summer sailing leaves Chelan mid-morning, reaches Stehekin around midday, and turns round after a layover of an hour or ninety minutes. That means a party arriving on the boat has half a day at most before the last sailing out, and a party finishing a climb has to be at the landing on the boat's schedule or spend another night. Book the boat and the permit together and treat the return sailing as a hard deadline. From the landing a valley shuttle runs eleven miles up to High Bridge, four times a day in each direction in season, and it is the second half of the same logistics problem — miss it and you are walking. Purple Point is where you sleep if the boat gets in too late to reach the upper valley, and Harlequin is where you sleep if you are heading for the Company Creek road in the morning. Neither serves a summit directly, and both are essential.
bivy.water: Purple Point has potable water and vault toilets. Harlequin has vault toilets, tables, fire rings and animal-resistant food lockers, with the Stehekin River alongside. Neither is a water problem.
bivy.permit: This is a two-jurisdiction valley and it matters. The landing and the lower road are in the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area; the upper valley and everything you climb from it are North Cascades National Park. A backcountry permit is required year round for every overnight in the park backcountry, and the valley campgrounds require a free permit as well. Permits are issued through the federal recreation booking site, with a lottery in early March, winners assigned booking dates through late March and April, and the general release at seven in the morning Pacific in late April. Roughly sixty percent of permits are reservable and forty percent held for walk-ups. There is no permit office in Stehekin — a walk-up permit has to be collected in person elsewhere in the park complex before you get on the boat, which is the trap that ends more trips here than weather. Bear canisters are not required at these particular camps but food must be stored in the lockers or hung; the valley has bears and they know the campgrounds. Purple Point was free for the 2026 season.
bivy.capacity: Purple Point has six walk-in tent sites about ten minutes on foot from the boat dock. Harlequin, four and a half miles up the valley road, has seven walk-in sites with shared parking. Both are first come, first served and both are small enough that a busy summer afternoon fills them.

itinerary: Day 1: Ferry/floatplane from Chelan to Stehekin Landing, NPS shuttle to Harlequin Bridge, then hike the Stehekin River Trail (~3 mi) and Devore Creek Trail (~4 mi, steep then brushy) to Bird Creek Camp (4,200 ft). Day 2: Round-trip summit push from Bird Creek Camp via the saddle south of Enigma Peak, Castle Creek crossing, and southwest ridge talus to the 8,323-ft summit and back (typically 6+ hours). Day 3: Hike out to Stehekin and catch the return ferry/shuttle. Many parties extend the trip to combine Flora with Devore and/or Tupshin Peaks from the same camp.

name: East Ledges
approach: Start at the Boston Basin trailhead off the Cascade River Road. A steep climbers' trail with several creek crossings (Boston Creek can run high on warm afternoons) climbs to the camps in Boston Basin; overnight stays there need a park backcountry permit. From the upper basin, head north toward Forbidden's South Face and climb the snow slopes and loose gully below and right of it to the East Ridge saddle just northwest of the Solitary Gendarme, about 8,300–8,400 ft. Allow about 4 hours from the trailhead to the saddle, or about 2 hours from the basin camps. Axe and crampons are usually needed for this snow; late in the season they can be left at the saddle.
descent: This route is itself a descent line. It rejoins the East Ridge crest at the solitary gendarme, from which parties descend the East Ridge's standard gully system back toward Boston Basin.

bivy.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
bivy.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
bivy.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

bivy.name: Boston Basin lower camp
bivy.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are no longer free — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
bivy.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

bivy.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
bivy.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Human waste must be packed out, and food still needs bear-resistant storage.
bivy.water: Entirely snowmelt and therefore seasonal. Early in the summer there is running water almost everywhere; by late season the high ground can be bare rock with nothing running, so plan to carry water up or melt snow.
bivy.permit: Still requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, from Marblemount. Whether an unestablished high bivouac is acceptable in Boston Basin is genuinely contested — the general zone regulation allows camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while the site-specific guidance for Boston Basin says to use the two designated camps. Ask when you collect the permit rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Party-sized ledges and snow platforms only; no facilities, no toilet, and no reliable flat ground once the snow has melted out.

itinerary: Used as the descent leg after climbing the West Ridge, East Ridge Direct, or North Ridge; not typically a stand-alone objective.

name: East Ridge
approach: From Trinity Trailhead, hike the Buck Creek Trail about 1.4 mi to the Chiwawa River Trail (#1550), then follow it north up the valley, staying left at the Red Mountain junction near 5 mi, to a ford of the Chiwawa River; beyond it a faint path leads to an avalanche chute, and open forest climbs cross-country to a basin near 5,500 ft and a bench near 6,300 ft, then traverse diagonally up toward Chiwawa Mountain's east ridge, descending to the roughly 7,200 ft col between Chiwawa and Fortress (or continuing over Chiwawa's summit first). Some parties instead approach via the Red Mountain Trail and Chiwawa Basin. From the col, a loose class 3-4 gully gains the crest of Fortress's East Ridge. The Chiwawa River has no usable bridge at the 4,800 ft meadow camp; in July parties wade it barefoot or in camp shoes, then bushwhack briefly before snow.
descent: Reverse the East Ridge and gully back to the Chiwawa-Fortress col, then descend to the bench and back down to the Chiwawa River/Buck Creek Trail to Trinity Trailhead.

bivy.name: Chiwawa Basin bench
bivy.notes: A flat heather bench in the upper Chiwawa basin between Fortress and Chiwawa, reached by a short climb from the end of the Chiwawa River trail. The usual high camp for the east side of Fortress and for Chiwawa.
bivy.water: Small streams on the bench; they can run low late in the season
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit
bivy.capacity: Several tent sites, some with rock windbreaks

bivy.name: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds
bivy.notes: These are staging camps, not climbing camps: the point of them is that the drive up the Chiwawa River road is around twenty-three miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, the last twelve are rough gravel and dirt genuinely unsuited to low clearance vehicles, and doing that at the end of a long drive from the west side is how parties end up starting the walk in tired and late. Phelps Creek Campground sits near the confluence of Phelps Creek and the Chiwawa a short distance below the Phelps Creek trailhead, and the Trinity trailhead at about 2,800 ft — the start of the Buck Creek trail toward Buck Creek Pass and Fortress Mountain — is a mile or so away, so one night here stages either objective. The road is the fragile part of this whole side of the zone. Storm damage has closed it above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year order, and a 2026 fire closure covered the Chiwawa River road and the Phelps Creek spur on top of that, so check whether you can drive to the trailhead at all before planning around it. When the road is shut above Atkinson Flat the lower campgrounds are still a reasonable base but the trailhead becomes a long walk or ride further on.
bivy.water: The Chiwawa River is right there but these are primitive campgrounds — treat water and expect no potable supply or trash service
bivy.permit: Small nightly fee at the developed sites, first come first served with no reservations, so arrive early on a summer Friday. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers trailhead parking the next morning, and the free self-issue wilderness permit is picked up at the trailhead itself. Fire restrictions bite here in late summer and often ban all open flame including in the fire rings.
bivy.capacity: Phelps Creek Campground has roughly seven tent sites plus half a dozen equestrian sites; Atkinson Flat, Schaefer Creek, Rock Creek and the other small forest campgrounds strung along the road below it each hold a handful more

itinerary: Typically a 2-3 day trip: hike in via the Chiwawa River/Buck Creek Trail to camp at the ~7,200 ft Chiwawa-Fortress col (or a 7,100 ft meadow plateau below Fortress), climb Fortress and often Chiwawa Mountain from camp, then hike back out. A car-to-car speed-traverse of both peaks (25+ miles, off-trail) has been done in just over 9 hours by a strong trail runner.

name: Southwest Face
approach: From Trinity Trailhead (2,800 ft) at the end of Chiwawa River Road/FR 6200, follow the Buck Creek Trail (#1513) roughly 9-9.5 miles, climbing through forest, an old avalanche debris field (~4,500 ft), and past an unmarked junction with the Pass No Pass way-trail (bears right, ~5,800 ft). Continue up the way-trail to Pass No Pass (~6,400 ft) and the alpine camping benches beyond, from which Fortress's southwest face and south ridge come into view. Note: storm damage has closed FR 6200 to vehicles beyond Atkinson Flat Campground (about mile 16), adding roughly 7 miles of road-walking each way before even reaching the trailhead; check its status with the Wenatchee River Ranger District.
descent: Descend the same southwest face/south ridge line; some parties prefer a cairned class 3 line on blocky terrain to skier's right of the ascent gully over down-climbing the loose gully directly.

bivy.name: Basin below Pass No Pass
bivy.notes: The small basin reached by the unmarked way trail that leaves the Buck Creek trail about a mile below Buck Creek Pass. The closest camp to the southwest face; the scramble starts above it.
bivy.water: Stream in the basin
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit
bivy.capacity: A few sites in a grove of trees and in the meadows

bivy.name: Buck Creek Pass
bivy.notes: The popular camp at the top of the Buck Creek trail, roughly ten miles from Trinity. From here drop back down the trail about a mile to the Pass No Pass way trail.
bivy.water: Stream near the pass
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit
bivy.capacity: Several forested sites near the pass

bivy.name: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds
bivy.notes: These are staging camps, not climbing camps: the point of them is that the drive up the Chiwawa River road is around twenty-three miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, the last twelve are rough gravel and dirt genuinely unsuited to low clearance vehicles, and doing that at the end of a long drive from the west side is how parties end up starting the walk in tired and late. Phelps Creek Campground sits near the confluence of Phelps Creek and the Chiwawa a short distance below the Phelps Creek trailhead, and the Trinity trailhead at about 2,800 ft — the start of the Buck Creek trail toward Buck Creek Pass and Fortress Mountain — is a mile or so away, so one night here stages either objective. The road is the fragile part of this whole side of the zone. Storm damage has closed it above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year order, and a 2026 fire closure covered the Chiwawa River road and the Phelps Creek spur on top of that, so check whether you can drive to the trailhead at all before planning around it. When the road is shut above Atkinson Flat the lower campgrounds are still a reasonable base but the trailhead becomes a long walk or ride further on.
bivy.water: The Chiwawa River is right there but these are primitive campgrounds — treat water and expect no potable supply or trash service
bivy.permit: Small nightly fee at the developed sites, first come first served with no reservations, so arrive early on a summer Friday. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers trailhead parking the next morning, and the free self-issue wilderness permit is picked up at the trailhead itself. Fire restrictions bite here in late summer and often ban all open flame including in the fire rings.
bivy.capacity: Phelps Creek Campground has roughly seven tent sites plus half a dozen equestrian sites; Atkinson Flat, Schaefer Creek, Rock Creek and the other small forest campgrounds strung along the road below it each hold a handful more

itinerary: Most parties make this a 2-3 day backpack: Day 1, hike in ~9-9.5 miles to camp at Buck Creek Pass or the alpine basin below Pass No Pass; Day 2, climb Fortress (very often combined with Buck Mountain and/or Chiwawa Mountain) from camp; Day 3, hike out. Fast parties have done it car-to-car in a single long day, with reported times ranging from under 12 hours up to about 19 hours when combined with other summits.

name: East Slope Route (Headlight Basin)
approach: From the Esmeralda Trailhead, hike the Esmeralda Basin Trail and Ingalls Way Trail up to Ingalls Pass (~6,500 ft), then traverse into Headlight Basin below the Ingalls/Fortune ridge.
descent: Downclimb or glissade the east-facing ascent slopes back into Headlight Basin (snow conditions permitting), then retrace over Ingalls Pass and out the Esmeralda Basin Trail.

bivy.name: Headlight Basin
bivy.notes: Open basin below Ingalls Pass on the Ingalls/Fortune ridge; the standard overnight base for this route, reached via the Esmeralda Basin and Ingalls Way trails.
bivy.water: Seasonal snowmelt/small streams; can be dry by late summer
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead
bivy.capacity: A handful of tent sites

itinerary: Often combined with North or South Ingalls Peak: Esmeralda Trailhead to Ingalls Pass, into Headlight Basin (sometimes camping there), up the east slope to the Fortune Peak summit, then reverse or continue to an adjacent peak before returning.

name: Standard Route (Esmeralda Basin – Lake Ann Pass)
approach: From the Esmeralda Trailhead (#1394, 4,269 ft), hike the Esmeralda Basin Trail (shared with the Lake Ingalls/Ingalls Way trail for the first 0.4 mi), then stay on the Esmeralda Basin Trail past the Ingalls Way junction to the trail toward Lake Ann. At the trail junction below the pass, head up toward Lake Ann and the saddle above it, then leave maintained trail and follow the ridge boot path to the summit.
descent: Reverse the ridge boot path back down to the pass above Lake Ann, then descend via the Ingalls Way/Esmeralda Basin Trail to the trailhead.

bivy.name: Lake Ann bench and the upper Esmeralda Basin camps
bivy.notes: The Esmeralda-side camp that is not Headlight Basin, and the one that actually serves the two peaks at the head of this valley. Esmeralda Peaks are scrambled directly from the basin on their standard route, and Fortune Peak's standard line goes up the basin and over the pass near Lake Ann before turning up the peak; both are honest day trips from the road end, so this is a place to sleep when the party is slow, the day is short, or you want two summits without driving twice. The trail leaves the road end at about 4,500 feet and climbs gently through meadow, timber and small stream crossings before the ground steepens toward the pass; take the Lake Ann branch to reach the bench and the knoll above it, which has a wide view back down the upper Teanaway. Fortune Peak can also be climbed by its east slope out of Headlight Basin, which is a different camp on the other side of the divide and is described with the Ingalls group rather than here. Mountain goats work this whole area and are bold about salt — keep gear packed and relieve yourself well away from camp.
bivy.water: The bench camp has running water beside it, fed by snowmelt draining the basin, and small streams cross the main basin trail lower down. All of it is snowmelt and all of it fades: reliable through July, marginal in August, and effectively gone by September, when the basin is dry rock and cured grass. There is no water at all on the pass or on either summit.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness above the basin, under the Cle Elum district and entirely outside the Enchantment Permit Area — a free self-issued slip from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use, with no quota, no lottery and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the Esmeralda Basin trailhead. No campfires; this is open subalpine meadow and the ban is both seasonal and permanent by elevation. Camping is prohibited at Ingalls Lake, which is a different basin over the divide, and the designated sites in Headlight Basin are the legal option on that side.
bivy.capacity: Small scattered sites rather than a campground — a bench part way up the Lake Ann branch takes a tent or two, and a knoll on its east side holds several more; nothing here suits a large group

itinerary: Typically a single long day: drive to the Esmeralda Trailhead, hike up the Esmeralda Basin Trail to the Ingalls Way junction, continue to the pass above Lake Ann, scramble the ridge to the summit, then reverse the entire route. Many parties combine it with South Ingalls Peak.

name: Infinite Bliss
approach: Park at the gravel pull-off (~47.54604, -121.52151, ~1,174 ft). Walk 100-200 yards farther east along the road to the climbers' path leaving on the left at a cairn, then hike about 45 minutes, mostly uphill through forest switchbacks, to the route start near 47.549, -121.5137.
descent: Rappel from the summit of Infinite Peak.
itinerary: A long single day is the norm: leave Seattle before dawn, be climbing by mid-morning, on the topout by mid-afternoon, back at the base by early evening. One documented fast ascent climbed the route in 5.5 hours (about 15 min/pitch, heavily simulclimbed), rappelled in 2.5 hours, and was back in Seattle by 9:30 p.m.; a typical strong party takes ~7 hours up and 3 hours down plus the approach.

name: Leaning Spire West Route
approach: Approach the same as the Main Peak's South Route to 'the Y', then turn up Gully #1 and follow it to the notch below the spire. Midway are 20 ft rock steps, climbable directly or bypassed via loose, brushy scrambling.
descent: Single 70m rope (60m likely sufficient) via 5+ rappels off trees and rock horns, with extensive down-scrambling. An alternative descent rappels off an overhang near the summit into Gully #2, though route-finding there is reported as 'quite scary.'
itinerary: One very long day, car to car, with a pre-dawn start; the shared South Route approach alone takes four to five hours to reach the Y, and a Main Peak round trip on the same terrain is rarely under twelve hours. A bivy at the Glade Saddle above the slab (room for two) turns it into a comfortable two-day trip and is the traditional option.

name: Preiss Route
approach: Hike basically straight up, taking a line of least resistance for roughly 1,500 ft while staying left of the lower rocky slabs, with up to 3rd-class scrambling. A 20 ft dirty downclimb leads to the base of the first pitch.
descent: Hike around right and scramble the short back side of the sub-summit rock, then descend up and over the main West Peak summit and down the west ridge; alternatively rappel with two ropes.
itinerary: A very long single day or a comfortable two-day trip. The large ledge under the steeper headwall, roughly two-thirds of the way up, is described as a great bivy site and is the natural split if you want to climb the headwall pitches fresh in the morning.

waypoints.name: Garfield Ledges trailhead — NF-110 spur leaves here; park about 1/3 mile up the spur

name: South Route (Main Peak)
approach: I-90 Exit 34 near North Bend, then the Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road (FR 56) past the Taylor River bridge junction to a pullout roughly 2.6 miles further on, by a gravel wash. From the car the whole route is only about 1.5 miles horizontally, but 4,400 vertical feet. Start up the dry creek bed and leave it partway up into the woods, following a mix of flagging tape and faint trail up steep pine-needle slopes — 'scrumbling', pulling on whatever vegetation is at hand. About an hour in, at roughly 2,200 ft, you reach the dirt gully. Note that the pine-needle slopes above the slab run about 40 degrees on loose duff; huckleberry stems make good handholds.
descent: Reverse the route: a single-rope rappel to the col and about four double-rope rappels down #2 Gully, then more raps on the wooded ramp and slab.
itinerary: Twelve hours is Beckey's stated absolute minimum and a fit, competent party should plan 15-17 hours car to car: one documented ascent left the car at 6:45 a.m., summited at 2:45 p.m., started down at 3:30 p.m. and reached the car at 11:05 p.m. The alternative is a two-day trip using the two-person bivy site at the Glade Saddle above the slab.

name: Southwest Ledges
approach: Leave the climber's path and head into steep forest, continuing upward nearly 1,000 ft through class 4 terrain and thick brush until dropping into a gully on the left; descend several hundred feet to reach the ledge system.
descent: Descend Infinite Bliss with two 60m ropes — roughly 20 rappels plus down-scrambling.
itinerary: Realistically a single enormous day: leave the car by first light, expect the better part of the day for the 2,600 ft of ledge navigation, and be on the summit early enough to start rappelling Infinite Bliss with hours of daylight in hand. Some parties bivy — ascents here generally need a bivouac or one of the longest days of summer.

waypoints.name: NF-110 gravel pull-off (Infinite Bliss / Southwest Ledges parking)
Base of Infinite Bliss — leave the climber's path here and head up into the forest

name: Gato Negro
approach: From the pullout, find a faint boot path descending loose talus/scree to the east into the trees, passing a trail register, then crossing Early Winters Creek on a log (~4,080 ft). The trail climbs the timbered rib north of Burgundy Creek, steeply gaining elevation to a basin/camp bench around 6,500 ft (roughly 2 hours from the car), where the trail continues on up to Burgundy Col (~7,720 ft). Whine Spire, just south of the Wine Spires, is reached from the bench rather than the col: branch right toward Silver Star and climb to the toe of the middle of the three rock masses to the right of the col. Good camping and a late-season spring are near 6,400-6,500 ft.
descent: Steep gully requiring 4th-class down-climbing with multiple rappels and loose rock throughout.

bivy.name: Burgundy Col high camp — west side, the Wine Spires
bivy.notes: The narrow saddle between Burgundy Spire and the ridge, and the standard high camp for the Wine Spires and for the Silver Star Glacier approached from the highway side. Published elevations disagree by a couple of hundred feet, with figures from roughly 7,720 to 7,950 in circulation, so treat any single number as approximate. It is exposed to wind from both sides and several parties have dropped back down the west slope to sleep after a rough night. Camping here removes about 1,500 ft of the scree from summit day, which is most of the argument for carrying overnight gear up it.
bivy.water: No spring or stream. Parties melt snow from the lingering patches on the glacier side of the col, which normally hold into late summer but can be rock-hard in the morning or gone entirely in a dry, late season. Many simply haul all their water up the scree, which is the single heaviest decision on this approach.
bivy.permit: None. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit, unlike the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
bivy.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

bivy.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — west side
bivy.notes: The flat, sheltered alternative to sleeping at the col, in trees before the timbered rib gives way to open scree. Reports consistently call it the more pleasant camp of the two, at the cost of extra vertical on summit morning. Elevation is quoted anywhere from about 6,400 to 6,500 ft depending on which flat spot a party used. Its value is almost entirely the spring: if that has failed, the bench loses most of its advantage over the col.
bivy.water: The most dependable water on this approach, but NOT from the obvious place. The creek shown on maps immediately east of the bench is frequently dry, while a spring roughly ten minutes north of camp keeps running well into September in most years. Confirm it before committing, and expect insects around it.
bivy.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, non-wilderness, so no permit or reservation applies.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots on a wooded bench, with a large boulder and an old fire ring as the usual landmark; comfortably three or four tents

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
bivy.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
bivy.water: No drinking water at the campground. Early Winters Creek runs alongside and needs filtering; Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds, farther east, have drinking water in season.
bivy.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
bivy.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles

bivy.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — west side
bivy.notes: Not an established campsite so much as a fallback for a party that has run out of daylight or water partway up the talus. The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.
bivy.water: Genuinely unreliable and conditions-dependent. At least one party found a trickle running here in a season when the bench camp creek below was dry, which makes it worth checking on the way up, but nothing about it is dependable enough to plan a camp around.
bivy.permit: None. Non-wilderness National Forest land; no permit, quota or registration.
bivy.capacity: Improvised, one or two small parties at most; flat ground has to be found or built rather than chosen

itinerary: Most parties base out of the bench camp (~6,500 ft) below the spire. Plan for: an early approach from camp to the base of the route, a full day on the 12 pitches (one fast party of four completed camp-to-camp, including the climb, in 9.5 hours), then the slow, loose descent gully (budget several hours). An alpine start is strongly recommended so the descent isn't finished in the dark.

waypoints.name: SR-20 Wine Spires / Silver Star pullout (~MP 166, ~4 mi east of Washington Pass)
Burgundy Creek bench camp — west side

name: Conrad Glacier
approach: From the South Tieton Creek/Conrad Meadows Trailhead, approach the north side of the peak and ascend the east side of Conrad Glacier to a saddle around 7,200 ft.
descent: Descend the ascent route back over the saddle and down Conrad Glacier.

bivy.name: Conrad Meadows and Surprise Lake, South Fork Tieton
bivy.notes: This is the correct side of the range for Gilbert Peak's Conrad Glacier and Meade Glacier routes, and there is no sensible way to reach either from the Snowgrass trailheads — the two approaches are separated by the whole crest. From the road end the trail runs level through meadows for around four miles before the loop divides, and the northern fork leads toward Surprise Lake and eventually the benches, waterfall and Barren Lake below the Conrad Glacier. Most parties camp once in the basin and climb from there, since the glacier and the traverse across the Meade to Gilbert's south ridge make for a long day on their own. The meadows at the road end are a legitimate first night if you arrive late, but they are low, buggy in early summer and a long way from anything. This side is far quieter than Snowgrass, and the corresponding cost is a much longer approach and much less traffic if something goes wrong.
bivy.water: The South Fork Tieton and its tributaries throughout, and the lake itself higher up; abundant by the standards of the range's east side but still to be treated
bivy.permit: Free self-issued wilderness permit at the trailhead board once you cross into the wilderness. Camping is prohibited within 100 feet of lakes. Note this trailhead sits on the drier eastern forest rather than the Gifford Pinchot side, so confirm which parking pass the board is asking for before leaving the car. Heavy stock use means the meadows are shared with horse parties.
bivy.capacity: Primitive dispersed and stock camping in the broad meadows at the road end, and established backcountry sites at Surprise Lake several miles up the loop; no reservations and no numbered sites

itinerary: Plan on two or more days car to car, given the extra distance of crossing both glaciers.

waypoints.name: Conrad Meadows Trailhead (South Fork Tieton Trail #1120)

name: Meade Glacier
approach: Drive to the Conrad Meadows / South Fork Tieton Trailhead (Trail #1120, elev. ~4,044 ft): from Naches, WA take US-12 W about 22 miles, turn onto Forest Road 1200 (Tieton Reservoir Road) for 4.5 miles, then onto Forest Road 1000 (South Fork Tieton Road) for 12.6 miles to the trailhead at road's end (last ~7 miles gravel, generally in good condition). Hike Trail #1120 through Conrad Meadows (crossing Conrad Creek) into the Goat Rocks Wilderness, continuing to the Surprise Lake loop. Take the loop's right fork to the trail's high point, then leave the trail and climb west into a basin; pass between a pair of big mounds and descend briefly to the foot of the Meade Glacier.
descent: Reverse the ascent route down the summit scramble, the Meade Glacier snowfields and the basin back to the Surprise Lake loop and Conrad Meadows Trail #1120.

Heavy stock use means the meadows are shared with horse parties.

itinerary: Typically done as an overnight/2-day backpack: Day 1, hike in to a camp at Surprise Lake (wooded, sheltered) or Warm Lake (above treeline, exposed to wind); Day 2, alpine start for the summit push across the basin and up the Meade Glacier snowfields, then return to camp and hike out (or split the hike-out over a 3rd day). Strong parties have done it car-to-car in a long single day.
